Moisture
mois´tūr
n. (sap, vital fluid; what a rooted thing draws and a rootless thing lacks — Hebrew lēach, Greek ikmas)
Latin mustum, new wine, through Old French moiste. The Hebrew lēach means freshness or sap; the Greek ikmas is moisture in the ground.

Biblical Definition

Moisture in Scripture is sap — the vital fluid that keeps a living thing green — and its absence is used three ways. In the parable of the sower, of the seed on rock: “And some fell upon a rock; and as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it lacked moisture” (Luk 8:6). The Lord Himself interprets it: “They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away” (Luk 8:13). Everything above ground was right — it sprang up quickly, and it was received with joy — and there was nothing beneath. David describes the same drying under conviction of sin: “For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer” (Psa 32:4) — the misery of unconfessed sin in a believer, which he ends in the next verse by acknowledging his transgression. And the word is used once as praise, of Moses at a hundred and twenty: “his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated” (Deu 34:7), where the Hebrew behind natural force is this same word for freshness. Moses died undimmed and unwithered, on the mountain, at the word of the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines moisture as a small quantity of any liquid; that which moistens or makes damp; and, of plants, the sap or juice which sustains life.

expand to see more

MOIST'URE, n. A small quantity of any liquid; that which moistens or makes damp.

2. In plants, the sap or vital juice; that without which vegetation cannot proceed.

MOIST, a. Moderately wet; damp; not dry.

SAP, n. The juice of plants of any kind, which nourishes and sustains the vegetable.

Key Scripture

Luke 8:6 — "And some fell upon a rock; and as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it lacked moisture."

Luke 8:13 — "They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away."

Psalm 32:4 — "For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah."

Deuteronomy 34:7 — "And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."

Modern Corruption

Quick and joyful response to the word is taken for conversion, when the Lord Himself names it as the mark of the rootless ground.

expand to see more

Luke 8:13 is one of the most sobering verses in the Gospels for anyone who measures ministry by response. The rocky ground produced the fastest growth of the four soils, and the reception was joyful; the Lord says of these that they for a while believe, and fall away in time of temptation. What was missing was invisible from the surface: root, and therefore moisture. Where a church counts its harvest by immediate enthusiasm, it will regularly report as fruit what Christ classifies as failure, and it will build methods designed to produce exactly the response He warns about.

The remedy is not to discourage joy. Both the second and the fourth soils receive the word; the difference is depth, and depth is a matter of what happens where no one is watching — in the closet, in the daily reading, in the hard obedience nobody applauds. David's dried-up moisture in Psalm 32 shows what it feels like when a real believer stops drinking: heaviness, wasting, the drought of summer, until he says I acknowledged my sin unto thee and the drought breaks. And Deuteronomy 34 shows the other end — a man of a hundred and twenty, undimmed and unwithered, because for forty years he had been drinking of that spiritual Rock that followed them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ikmas (G2429), moisture in the soil — Luke 8:6 only; Hebrew lēach (H3893), freshness, sap, natural force — Deuteronomy 34:7; lěshad (H3955), moisture or vital juice — Psalm 32:4.

expand to see more

Greek ikmas (G2429) — moisture; Luke 8:6, its only occurrence in the New Testament.

Hebrew lēach (H3893) — freshness, moisture, natural force; Deuteronomy 34:7, Jeremiah 11:16 of the green olive tree.

Hebrew lěshad (H3955) — sap or vital moisture; Psalm 32:4, Numbers 11:8 of the taste of the manna.

Greek rhiza (G4491) — root; what the rocky ground lacked, and the reason the moisture failed.

Psalm 1:3 and Jeremiah 17:8 give the opposite case: a tree planted by the waters whose leaf shall be green.

Usage

"“It withered away, because it lacked moisture” — and it had sprung up fastest."

"“Which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away”."

"“Nor his natural force abated” — Moses undimmed at a hundred and twenty."
